thread.title: Apple: Glass Half Full Or Half Empty - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Reel Ken
title: Apple: Glass Half Full Or Half Empty - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Well, we certainly have been given a wild ride - for the markets and for Apple ( AAPL ) in particular. As I speak to investors and professionals, many seem to be in a form of "shock". I don't blame them. When one experiences historic moves - up and down - moves that occur within days coupled with extreme intra-day swings - investors are being confronted with new territory.
Now, there are plenty of pundits that will try to explain the movements and offer some reason - real or imagined. The problem I have with them is not just the divergence in thought, but it is nearly impossible to apply rational explanation to a dysfunctional market.
What investors need to recognize is that with pundits as ubiquitous as they are, one can find support for almost any theory or prediction. Add to that mix the fact that most investors truly seek out confirmation of predispositions. Investors have an uncanny ability to find that which they want to find rather than that which they need to know.
With that said, I'm not going to offer some deep analysis or unique explanation for the market or for AAPL. There are already more than enough of those. Instead, I want to share my experience and how I'm positioning myself. The thought processes that guided my decision making. It is my hope that readers can identify with the process or parts of the process. If so, they can potentially take away a winning actionable plan. Not an actionable plan that will fit everyone - but one that seemed just right for me. Maybe you, too.
My regular readers know that I trade mostly option strategies and had only one pure stock - AAPL (though I did recently add Amazon ( AMZN )). As far as AAPL goes, I was a little late to the party having bought in at $112. I saw it as a buy-and-hold-forever position.
Then, after just a few years, AAPL started a meteoric climb, and by April 2018, it had reached $170. I was torn - on the one hand, I had nice gains and on the other hand were hopes for more to come. After experiencing the psyche struggle between fear and greed, I eventually reached what I thought was a rationally based decision. AAPL's climb caused a concentration risk and some form of paring was the "book" thing to do. For when a position size gets too big, it adds an extra layer of risk - a layer above and beyond any inherent risk the stock may have. After all, we often assume market risk - but it's not too good an idea to compound that risk with portfolio risk.
Now, many may consider it "old school" that one should not put more than 5% of their risk assets in any one security. As AAPL was my only actual stock (the rest being options), I chose a 5% initial allocation towards it. So, with a 60% growth to $170/share, the allocation grew to somewhat over 7%.
Many investors face this problem. How much and when should they pare back a winner? Though many pundits propose "let winners ride", they do so without taking into account the overall portfolio. In AAPL's case, the concentration risk was starting to scream louder than the bull story.
Even so, greed dominated and influenced my decision. I decided that I'd let AAPL run up a little more before I sell out. After all, the prospects looked bright. And, as far as analysts go - well, I could find as many bulls as bears. I knew I had to reduce somewhat but greed had my ear. Selling a slightly out-of-the-money covered call a year or so away seemed to fit the bill. Greed dictated not being too cautious and I decided to sell a covered call on just 1/2 my position. I chose a $180 strike and an expiry a year away - June 21, 2019.
That gave me a $10 potential run up in stock price alone and by choosing a June 21, 2019 expiry, the premium credit was $13. That meant I had a 7.5% buffer to the downside ($13/$170) and nearly a 14% upside ($10+$13=$23/170 =13.5%). AAPL, I mused, might climb higher than this but certainly wasn't going any lower! And, of course, since it was just 1/2 my position, the sky was the limit on the other 1/2. I was able to assuage both the need to reduce position size and greed impulses.
Seemed reasonable. But, soon after, AAPL continued its climb and went upwards of $225. Naturally, I kicked myself for having "lost the faith" by selling the covered call. Though the covered call was more than 30% deep-in-the-money, there was still about $5 in extrinsic value. All I had to do was wait it out till June 21 and earn that "extra" $5 as well as the dividends paid along the way. It seemed a pretty easy decision to "let it ride" till June 2019 and ultimately be called away at $180. After all, with AAPL at $225 what could go wrong?
However, soon thereafter AAPL dropped to $205 and I was thinking maybe "all that glitters...". Fear/greed, once again in play. This time fear won out and I sold the 1/2 that was not subject to the covered call at $205. That left me with a DITM $180 strike covered call. My rationale centered, once again, around concentration risk. AAPL at $205 represented almost 10% of my portfolio and I could no longer let greed dominate. Fundamental investing technique - which is a derivative of discipline - has to take charge.
To my chagrin, I've stood by and watch AAPL fall relentlessly into the $140s. Glad I sold at $205, sorry I didn't close out the other 1/2 at the same time. Both decisions seemed right at the time. So far, only one turned out the winner.
Like so many others, I ran the emotional gambit in very short time frame. Sensibility, fear, greed, more fear and now - I don't know what - a sense of confusion. Almost a paralysis. Like so many others, I made good moves and not so good moves along the way. Overall, I pocketed healthy profits and my remaining shares are still 50% above cost basis.
So - and this is the real question - why do I feel like a loser? Yes, by every objective criterion, I'm a big winner. But, and here's the key, I believe that the uncertainty in not knowing what to do now creates anxiety that taints my view.
So, I'm back to trying to look at it objectively. Here's where I landed and what I did:
1) Back in April 2018, I was willing to sell out my position at $180 when I sold the covered call. If I was willing to sell out at $180, then, why not now?
2) I gained $10 of the $13 so far on the covered call so selling, now at $170, would generate the same as selling them at $180. In short - if I was willing to sell them at a given price, then I should be willing to sell, today, at the same net price.
3) I believe AAPL is oversold. Note that this is a belief, not an objective determination. Instead of following the traditional trail of accepting what pleases me, I choose to acknowledge that, in the end, it is what I believe that drives the decision-making process.
Certainly, the fact that I own AAPL influences my decisions. I've written about this phenomenon previously , so I won't expand upon it in this article. I point this out, mainly, because investors need to understand when their decisions are based upon belief and not fool themselves into thinking it's some higher intellect at work.
4) If AAPL is oversold, then a bull strategy fits more soundly than a neutral strategy.
5) I still operate with fear and though I know I should go more bull, fear talks me out of it. In order to reconcile these issues, I seek out a strategy that will sell out at $170, not risk any more than I already have at risk and at the same time, employ a bull strategy.
The Action Plan Those that follow me know that I see things in terms of option metrics. Options allow me to construct a result that fits my objective. There is one particular strategy that fits both AAPL and my objectives to a tee: the ratio call spread.
Here's how that works:
1) Buy a call at a strike of $140 with an expiry of June 2019. That costs $17.60. The number of calls (x100) should equal the number of AAPL shares.
2) Sell twice as many calls at a strike of $155 and the same expiry of June 2019 for a credit of $9.65, each. The total credit for the 2x call option is $19.30.
3) The combination of the two option steps - the buy and the 2x sale - results in a net credit of $1.70 ($19.30-$17.60).
Possible Outcomes 1) AAPL lands below $140 on June 21st. Naturally, there is additional loss on the stock. However, the option strategy has both calls expiring worthless for a net gain of $1.70. I took a shot, I lost, but I gained.
2) AAPL lands between $140 and $155. I earn $1 for every dollar that AAPL lands above $140. For instance, AAPL is now trading around $148. If that holds till June, that puts the $140 call, $8 in the money and I earn $8 plus the net premium credit of $1.70 for a total gain of $9.70. This gain represents a 6.5% return if AAPL goes nowhere! If AAPL goes as high as $155, the gain is $7 on the stock ($155-$148) and $15 on the ratio spread.
Let's examine that more closely. I've made $1 for each $1 above $140 and still have my AAPL stock. I can just re-institute the ratio call spread for another expiry and other strikes.
3) AAPL lands above $155. Since there are two short calls at $155 and only one long call at $140, there is no further gain from either the ratio spread or the stock, itself. The short calls zero out any future appreciation.
But, let's examine more closely what happens if AAPL lands above $155. The stock holding is sold (assigned) by virtue of one of the short calls at $155. However, the $140 call is $15 in-the-money and that represents $15 in gains. And let's not forget the option credit of $1.70. Add that credit to the $15 from the long call and the option strategy made $16.70 net. When added to the $155 call price on the basic stock and the strategy is equivalent to selling out at $171.70.
Here's a chart that may help to clarify. Keep in mind that this chart illustrates the outcomes for AAPL with and without the call ratio spread.
The blue line represents AAPL plus the call ratio and the green line AAPL, alone using AAPL's current trading price of $148 as the start point and expiry of June 21st.
Consistent with the prior discussion, one can see that the call ratio spread does provide a down buffer and if a sale is triggered, it is at an equivalent price of $170. Also, of note, is the gain if AAPL never moves above the current $148.
The Key Now, I didn't just pick these strikes and expirations out of a hat. The first step was my willingness to sell out my position if AAPL hit $170. I then simply looked at various strikes, with the upper leg - the 2x short call - approximately half the price of the lower long call. That way, the combination of the two results in an approximate zero net cost.
Next, I looked at the distance between the two strikes so that the short calls are mid-way between the long call and $170. It turned out to be $140/$155 with $155 mid-way between $140 and $170. On other days and other expirations, it could have turned out at $150/$160 or $120/$145 or many others. But in each scenario, the important part is that the 2x short call sits mid-way between the long call and the desired "sell-out" target.
So, there's a little art and science involved. Those that are very familiar with options may choose slightly different variations - of which, there are countless - I'm just illustrating the one I chose.
Of course, one could manage for more upside potential or more downside protection. The beauty about options is the ability to construct a result given the parameters one wished to establish. There is no "one size fits all" as one's goals and outlook are driving forces.
For instance, one could just write a simple covered call to provide a greater down buffer at the expense of making less upside. Since my "belief" is that AAPL is oversold, the call ratio provides more upside than a covered call, albeit with less of a downside buffer.
Summary What I've tried to accomplish with this article is to bare the thoughts that went through my mind at various stages of my AAPL ownership. The thought process is often emotionally driven and getting back to fundamental investing techniques can help overcome the fear/greed cycle.
Additionally, I've laid out my action plan. I'm willing to sell out at $180 net. That willingness to set a target price and the fortitude to stand by it enables creation of an options strategy that can multiply my interim returns.
It is not so much that this particular strategy fits everyone - or even most - but that by sticking to sound investment technique - establishing goals and parameters - one can use options to create a positive outcome.
Most importantly, in times of uncertainty and especially after seeing a stock holding rise or/and fall up to 50% in a short period of time, it can be helpful and soothing to rethink how the position fits one's portfolio.
Instead of just sitting idly by and thinking "what if " I'd have done this or that - instead one can always reflect back on fundamental strategies and not forget that they can still manage their positions. Doing so helps one feel less like a victim and more like an investor.
Disclosure: I am/we are long AAPL. I wrote this article myself, and it expresses my own opinions. I am not receiving compensation for it (other than from Seeking Alpha). I have no business relationship with any company whose stock is mentioned in this article.
